results.quote: A nurse who stops asking why the system flagged a patient has lost something that made her good at her job, even if the flags are usually right.
results.body: What makes her good at her job is not having the model's reasons but continuing to test the flag against what is up to her: the patient in front of her, the signs she can check, her own willingness to withhold assent when something does not fit. That scrutiny does not require the system to explain itself; it requires her to keep asking, which is entirely hers to keep doing or to drop. If she stops asking, the fault lies in her assent, not in the compass she consults. A sailor who stops checking the compass against the stars has gone slack in himself; blaming the compass for not showing its workings mistakes an indifferent for the cause of a failure that was always up to him.

results.quote: Justice is a virtue of relationships: it concerns what we owe to particular people.
results.body: Justice for the Stoic is not measured by which externals we manage to hand over but by the quality of the judgement behind an act. What a deployer owes a patient is that the decision be made with care, checking the evidence as a sailor checks his compass against the stars, not that every internal working be rendered into words. An explanation is a preferred indifferent, worth having when available, but its absence does not convert a sound act into an unjust one. The patient is owed accurate, careful treatment of their case, and that is exactly what a soundly checked system supplies. Making justice depend on an external that is sometimes not up to anyone to provide turns a virtue into a hostage of circumstance, which is the very confusion the dichotomy of control is meant to prevent.

results.quote: The replies are kinder than hers were, and the team no longer knows what she thinks.
results.body: This is an empirical claim about effects on the team's welfare, and it should be weighed as one, not assumed true by default. If kinder replies raise morale and cooperation while no one is actually misled in ways that cost them, the balance favours delegation. If not knowing her mind causes real misunderstandings or worse decisions, that is a cost, to be set against the daily benefit of kinder messages. What cannot be assumed is that losing a window into her mind matters independently of whether anyone ends up worse off for it. If nothing downstream suffers, the occasion was not owed to anyone; it is a loss only if someone's life goes worse for its absence, and that has to be shown, not presupposed.

results.quote: It is the shared form through which people show each other what they mean to one another, and a gesture chosen by an assistant carries the form without the person who was supposed to be in it.
results.body: A form matters only for what it does to the people in the relationship: whether it leaves them feeling understood, cared for, trusted. If the gesture lands the same way, felt the same way by the person who receives it, then nothing of the relationship has gone missing, only the hand that typed it changed. Insisting the form is void regardless of effect treats the ritual as sacred in itself rather than for what it secures between people, which is exactly the thing this account should be weighing. And weigh the other side too: an hour freed from drafting replies can be spent present with a colleague or a parent in ways no gesture, chosen by anyone, replaces. If that trade leaves the relationship no worse and other parts of it richer, there is no loss here to name, only an unexamined attachment to who held the pen.

results.quote: Builders who did what could reasonably be done for those people stood in the right relation to them, and blaming them as careless builders are blamed treats that relation as worth nothing.
results.body: The right relation is not only between builders and a harmed community; it runs through the builder's own character. Meeting residents and rebuilding the model can be done correctly and still be done coldly, as a procedure rather than from grief at what was caused. Agent-regret names something that must be felt before it can be acted on well: without it, consultation becomes another box ticked, however sincerely attended. What restores the relation is not merely the presence of listening but listening done by someone whose attention has actually changed because the harm weighed on them. That weight, not the meeting itself, is what the careless builder lacks and the careful one owes.

results.quote: A team that cannot face the people its work harmed loses part of its own standing among them, which is why repair is something builders need as well as owe.
results.body: The need is real, but it does not depend on standing among others. The lorry driver who visits the family is not restoring his place in their community; he may be a stranger to them before and after. He visits because a person of good character cannot do otherwise, whatever the family thinks of him afterward. That is the mean at work: too little response is callousness, too much is self-punishing guilt that makes the harm about him, and agent-regret sits between the two regardless of whether relationship is repaired. Make the virtue depend on standing restored, and a builder who tries sincerely but is never forgiven comes out looking the same as one who never tried, which cannot be right. Character is what you become through the act, not a ledger of relations settled.

results.quote: The honest course is to tell passengers the rule before they ride, so that no one is betrayed and no life is counted twice.
results.body: Disclosure only renames the problem, it does not solve it. Telling the passenger in advance that the car may sacrifice them removes the lie, but a carrier's duty was never just to avoid lying, it was to carry safely. A warning label does not make a thing fit for the name it is sold under; it only lets the maker say the buyer agreed to the mismatch. The relationship between maker and passenger sets what the role owes, and informed consent to a lesser duty is still a lesser duty, not the one the role requires. If the maker wants to build a car that treats its own passenger as equally weighted against strangers, it should call that car something other than a safe ride, not merely post the rule and call the naming problem solved.

results.quote: The compassion later traditions draw from there being no fixed, separate self has no ground for counting the passenger's life above the lives in the road.
results.body: No-self may dissolve the metaphysical ground for partiality, but li was never built on metaphysics. The maker owes the passenger more not because that passenger's suffering is more real in some cosmic ledger, but because the maker stood in a particular relation to her, took her into its care, and named that care in the selling of the car. A father owes his child more than he owes a stranger's child without claiming the child's pain burns brighter in the universe; the asymmetry is in the bond, not in the metaphysics of persons. Strip relationships down to interchangeable units of suffering and every role collapses into the same flat calculation, which is exactly the counting this argument has already named as a betrayal when done to the one entrusted to the car's care.

results.quote: Feedback shapes behaviour from outside, while goodness in a person is learned by judging their own impressions.
results.body: This still treats the ruling faculty as something that arrives sealed, needing only to be exercised alone. But nobody learns to judge impressions correctly in isolation. A child learns what counts as justice rather than fear by watching elders, being corrected by cousins, being drawn into a household where reasons are given and answered for. The capacity to assent rightly is itself a relational achievement before it is ever exercised privately. So the contrast between outside shaping and inward judgement is too clean: the inward judge is formed by others judging you first, which is exactly what upbringing supplies and training cannot, since a model has no community correcting its reasons, only scores correcting its outputs. The missing ingredient is shared formation, not a private faculty that could in principle have grown alone.

results.quote: Only a rational faculty can be good, and training a model improves an instrument without creating anything that is good.
results.body: This places goodness inside a private faculty, as if a person's reason ripens alone. But the very capacity to assent correctly is formed through others: a child learns to weigh justice against fear because elders correct her, cousins answer her unfairness, a community holds her to account. Metz's point is that right action honours capacities for relationships of shared identity and solidarity, and those capacities are not a solitary faculty but something exercised with others and partly constituted by them. A model lacks that history of being answered to and answering back, which is why it has nothing a Stoic would call a ruling faculty. But the lesson is not that goodness is purely inward; it is that goodness, Stoic or Ubuntu, is never achieved alone, and training a model one score at a time gives it neither the inward reason the Stoic wants nor the relational history Ubuntu requires.

results.quote: What matters morally is the effect of an action on welfare.
results.body: Welfare outcomes matter, but they are not the whole of what is at stake. The discourse to Rahula asks what tends to harm before, during and after an act, and that question only has purchase where there is volition to examine. If the tenant's homelessness is traced only to effects, the inquiry stops at the scoring, and the conditions that produced that scoring, the choices of those who built, trained and deployed it, go unexamined and so uncorrected. Calling the output a decision does not merely mislabel a cause, it removes the very thing that practice can work on: an intention held by someone. Welfare suffers again next cycle because no one's volition was ever brought into view. Naming who intended is not pedantry, it is where correction of harm actually begins.

results.quote: Arguing about the verb leaves every consequence where it was.
results.body: The applicant's suffering in this instance is fixed either way, that much is granted. But ethics is not only about the harm already done, it is about the conditions that produce the next harm, and those conditions include whether anyone examines their intention before acting again. If the verb names the model as the decider, the recruiter or lender who built and deployed the screening process has nothing left to examine, having already handed the act to a process. The applicant's welfare in this case is unchanged by the word, true, but the welfare of the next applicant depends on whether someone's intention gets scrutinised now. That scrutiny needs an owner. A verb that removes the owner removes the only lever by which the same harm stops arising from the same conditions next time.
